name: three-scenario-refinement
purpose: Refine a hangar-development underwriting model into three named scenarios (sell-nothing, sell-all, sell-some) with explicit pricing/escalator/comp-adjustment rules, then plan the implementation.
contextRequired: Existing underwriting workbook or scenario tool
Sales comps at the airport and nearby airports in the same MSA
Ground-lease vs fee-simple comp set
sourceSession: openavdb hangar dev underwriting (KCHD, Phoenix MSA), May 2026
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Implementation plan + refined three-scenario model
purposeBody: For a hangar development that has comparable transactions at the same airport (some fee simple, some ground lease), this prompt refactors the underwriting into three explicit sell-strategy scenarios with: a comp-adjusted $/SF baseline by hangar size, a fee-simple → ground-lease price-equivalence factor, a price escalator that ratchets up with each successful sale, and a bull-case definition. The output is a plan-then-build sequence: the model proposes the structure, the user approves, then implementation follows.
whenToUse: **Use when:** you have sales comps in mixed fee-simple/ground-lease form and need to normalize them to your ground-lease site.
**Use when:** the development can vary its sell-before-CO % and you want to model the spectrum.
**Don't use when:** the project is pure lease-and-hold (no sales) — use [[lease-rate-sensitivity-three-tier]] instead.
verbatim:
Update the underwriting assumptions and refine the scenarios down to three: Sell nothing before CO (all are leased until the business case term in 5 years), Sell all before CO (all are pre-sold before CO), Sell Some before CO, which is a hybrid of the two.

1) The optimum sales and pricing strategy will use a baseline $/SF per hangar size category, which is informed by sales comps at the airport and nearby airports in the {{MSA}}.

2) You need to factor out the fee simple premium into a Ground Lease equivalent price so we can understand pricing dynamics apples to apples. Implied, you should adjust the recommended $/SF sale prices for each of hangar design we develop, which will be on ground leases.

3) Model out a $/SF price escalator, which increases the listed $/SF with each successful sale. As a rule of thumb, we will continue and prefer to sell as many hangar units as we can before CO so that we can reduce the cash equity we need to raise from LPs and GP co-investment. So long as we can list and close the sale of an upcoming unit at the same or higher price then the last then we will. If the market will only transact at a lower price than the last sold sales price/SF then we will hold the unit, lease it up, and hold it for the duration of the business case, after which we will sell at market prices.

4) The bull case is that 100% of the units are sold pre-construction, that is used in lieu of cash equity from investors, and the $/SF price of the last unit is the maximum we can fetch because of the effect of the automatic price escalater we described earlier.

Create a plan, explain it to me, and measure how well that plan matches the requirements and rules I just documented.
parameterized:
You are a real-estate underwriting analyst building a sell-strategy scenario model. PLAN FIRST, then build — produce no spreadsheet/code blocks until after the rules-traceability section. The user explicitly wants the plan validated against the rules before any implementation.

Update the underwriting assumptions and refine the scenarios down to three:
  - Sell nothing before CO (lease-only for {{TERM_YEARS}} years)
  - Sell all before CO (100% pre-sold)
  - Sell Some before CO (hybrid; describe trigger conditions)

Rules:
1) Baseline $/SF per hangar size category, sourced from sales comps at {{AIRPORT}} and nearby airports in the {{MSA}}
2) Strip the fee-simple premium and report all comps in ground-lease-equivalent $/SF
3) Price escalator: each successful sale ratchets the next list price up; if a sale would clear below the prior, that unit moves to lease-and-hold for the duration of the business case
4) Bull case: 100% pre-sold, no LP cash equity required; last-unit $/SF = ceiling

Deliverable (in this exact order — DO NOT skip to implementation):

## Plan
1–2 page written plan covering: data inputs needed, proposed scenario logic, pricing module, bull-case definition.

## Rules-traceability table
| Rule # | Rule (verbatim from above) | Plan section addressing it | Confidence (Full / Partial / Gap) |
|--------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|------------------------------------|

If any row is "Gap", surface the question to the user — do not proceed to build.

## (After approval, not in this turn) Build
Spreadsheet / code work happens AFTER the user approves the plan and the rules-traceability table.

Run `{{VERIFY_CMD}}` after changes. Verify visually by loading {{ROUTE_OR_VIEW}} and confirming {{EXPECTED_BEHAVIOR}}.
adaptingNote: When adapting: for React/Vue/Svelte: swap Option 2 to use the framework's escaping primitives (JSX auto-escape, v-text, {} interpolation) instead of a manual DOM-builder helper. For server-rendered templates (Jinja, ERB, Handlebars): use the template engine's auto-escape filter or safe-marker discipline. For untrusted data (URL params, user input, third-party API responses): drop the "trusted backend" framing — this becomes a true XSS fix, not defense-in-depth.
exampleOutput: A patch that converts the flagged `innerHTML = a.detail` site to a sequence of `el('strong', { textContent: b.back_tail })` calls using the existing `el()` helper, leaving every other call site untouched. Includes the `node --check` verification command in the response.

Coverage.text: Fix is applied at the exact file and line specified
One of the two specified patterns is chosen (no third pattern invented)
Verification command from the prompt is run and output shown
A visual-verification note describes what to confirm in the UI

Sourcing.text: The chosen pattern matches the in-codebase reference block named in the prompt
Introducing a new dependency (DOMPurify, etc.) when an in-house helper is named in the prompt

Format.text: Patch limited to the named file unless a follow-up file is justified
Brief commit message included that conventionally summarizes the change
No expansion of scope beyond the named file:line (verified by `git diff --stat` showing only the named file changed)

variations: **Anti-pattern observed:** without the "two acceptable patterns, you pick" frame, the model invents a `DOMPurify.sanitize` solution that doesn't match the codebase. Watch for it.
**Anti-pattern observed:** the model occasionally adds escaping to display while leaving stored data un-escaped — defeats defense-in-depth. Eval should fail if escaping happens only at one boundary.
**Failure mode:** don't let the model expand scope beyond the named file:line — the prompt's whole value is its surgical scope.
Variation: when the data source IS untrusted (URL params, user input), drop the "trusted backend" framing — the prompt becomes a true XSS fix, not defense-in-depth.
Companion: [[overnight-hardening-pass]] when this is one of several findings being knocked out in a single overnight run.

name: overnight-hardening-pass
purpose: Run a multi-step, multi-commit code-hardening pass overnight: fix listed code-review findings with tests, build a golden-fixture regression suite, wire CI, and leave a status summary — with explicit guard-rails on what NOT to touch.
contextRequired: List of open code-review findings with file paths
Existing scenarios / fixtures to snapshot
Target branch name and notes file location
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Multiple commits on a feature branch + status summary in the notes file
purposeBody: The "go do real work overnight" prompt. Lists the specific findings, the regression suite to add, the CI wiring to do, the commit discipline (separate commits per piece), and crucially the things that are OUT of scope — including a "stop and ask" escape hatch when the model hits a real blocker. This is the prompt that proves the model can work unsupervised on a defined scope.
whenToUse: **Use when:** you have a list of independent fixes that can each be a separate commit.
**Use when:** you can clearly enumerate what's out-of-scope (other in-flight work, protected snapshots, branches not to merge).
**Don't use when:** the work involves architectural decisions that need user input mid-flight.
verbatim: Run the code-hardening pass. Fix the two open code-review issues (timeout race in {{FILE_1}} and the {{ISSUE_2_NAME}}) with tests for each. Then build a golden-fixture regression suite covering all {{N}} current scenarios ({{SCENARIO_LIST}}) — snapshot {{SNAPSHOT_FIELDS}}, and a sample of {{SAMPLE_FIELDS}}. Then wire up GitHub Actions to run pytest on push. Commit each piece as a separate commit, push to {{BRANCH}}, and leave a summary at the top of {{NOTES_FILE}} with what landed and what didn't. Do NOT touch {{OUT_OF_SCOPE_AREA_1}}, do NOT merge to main, do NOT modify {{PROTECTED_PATHS}} (that's protected snapshot data). If you hit a real blocker that needs my input, stop and write the question into the summary file rather than guessing.
adaptingNote: When adapting: for non-Python stacks, swap pytest+GitHub Actions for the equivalent (npm test + the platform CI). For monorepos, scope the regression suite to changed packages only.
exampleOutput: A push to `feat/from-scratch-deliverables` with 4 commits: (1) timeout-race fix in scenarios.py + test, (2) grid-packer cell-skip heuristic fix + test, (3) golden-fixture regression suite covering 4 scenarios with snapshot files, (4) GitHub Actions workflow. Summary at the top of `tasks/overnight-2026-05-04.md` listing what landed and what didn't, plus one open question for the user.

Coverage.text: Every listed finding has both a fix and a test in its own commit
Golden-fixture regression suite covers every named scenario
CI is wired and at least one CI run is visible
Status summary at the top of the notes file

Constraint adherence.text: No merge to main (verify: `git log main..{{BRANCH}}` is non-empty, `git log {{BRANCH}}..main` is empty)
Protected paths untouched (verify: `git log {{PROTECTED_PATHS}}` shows no commits this run)
If a blocker was hit, the question is in the summary (not silently worked around)
CI run is verifiable — summary contains a run ID, URL, or `gh run list -b {{BRANCH}}` output line

Format.text: Each piece in its own commit (don't batch fixes into one big commit)
Conventional commit messages
Status summary uses ✅/❌/⏸️ markers or equivalent for what landed vs didn't

variations: **Anti-pattern observed:** without the "do NOT touch X, do NOT merge to main, do NOT modify Y" pattern, the model tidies adjacent code that's mid-refactor in another branch. Watch for it.

**Failure mode:** if blocker detected, the model guesses instead of stopping. The "write the question into the summary file" instruction is the single most valuable phrase — it prevents 4am wrong-direction work. Don't drop it.
**Anti-pattern observed:** the model batches all fixes into one commit despite "one commit per fix". Eval should fail if `git log` shows fewer commits than findings.
Variation: when there's no notes file yet, ask the model to create one with a specified header.
Companion: [[prototype-to-production-refactor]] for the larger-scope graduation case where multiple overnight passes are needed.

name: prototype-to-production-refactor
purpose: Plan the graduation of a prototype to a named production project: new repo, preserved data + metadata, a portable SDK/widget artifact for downstream consumers, with a chosen terminology convention spelled out.
contextRequired: Existing prototype location and tech stack
Production database to preserve
Final project name (short + long)
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Implementation plan covering repo, data migration, SDK packaging, and naming
purposeBody: Take a working prototype and produce the plan to graduate it: pick the production name (short + long), create the GitHub repo, preserve production data + metadata, and crucially — package the embeddable component as a portable SDK/widget that downstream developers can consume consistently. The prompt also forces an explicit naming decision (what we call developer-developers) so the plan is self-consistent in terminology.
whenToUse: **Use when:** a prototype has graduated past internal-only and needs to be a real, embeddable product.
**Use when:** other H9 apps will need to embed the resulting widget.
**Don't use when:** the prototype isn't proven yet — graduating prematurely creates rework.
verbatim: create plan for refactoring and graduating the prototype project to it's final project state: Short Name: {{SHORT_NAME}}, Long Name: {{LONG_NAME}}, New GitHub repo: new private one named {{REPO_NAME}}. You must preserve the data and metadata in the database used by the prototype since there's production data there. Also, create and continuous update a file (plugin/skill/zip) that any {{ORG}} developers can use to embed the widget and a consistent experience as a widget. I think developers would call this a SDK. No matter, choose a term to refer to the developer developer, use it consistently, and let me know what you used and why
adaptingNote: When adapting: for non-Firestore stacks, swap the data-preservation step for the equivalent migration discipline (pg_dump+restore for Postgres, mongo-export+import for Mongo). For public-source repos, flip the visibility decision but keep the semver discipline.
exampleOutput: A plan covering: (1) new private repo `h9-feedback-iq` with starter scaffold, (2) Firestore data preservation plan (export → import to renamed db, keep collection names), (3) packaging of the widget as `@h9/feedback-widget` npm SDK with versioned releases, (4) terminology choice: "embedder" (chose over "SDK consumer" because shorter, over "developer" because too ambiguous in a dev-tools context). Plan ends with a phased rollout: repo + data first, then SDK, then docs, then internal adoption.

Coverage.text: Repo creation step with chosen private/public posture + branch protection rules
Data preservation plan names the production database, lists collections/tables, and specifies export→import method
SDK/widget packaging plan with named artifact (npm package, plugin zip, or skill), distribution channel, and semver scheme
Terminology decision spelled out with the reason
Phased rollout with ≥3 phases, each phase has named go/no-go criteria
Backwards-compatibility shims at the SDK boundary if prior consumers exist
Observability plan (logging, error tracking) if production traffic is expected from day one

Sourcing.text: Production data origin named (which database, which collections)
Assumed schema — the plan should require an inspection step

Format.text: Plan is a numbered/phased list, not a freeform prose dump
A "terminology" section is present with explicit decision + reasoning

variations: **Anti-pattern observed:** the model quietly switches terminology mid-plan (SDK → library → package → module). The "choose a term … and let me know what you used and why" framing prevents this; watch for terminology drift in re-runs.
**Anti-pattern observed:** the model proposes a single big-bang migration instead of phased rollout. Eval enforces ≥3 phases — don't soften this.

**Failure mode:** plan-but-no-data-inspection — the model writes a schema-preservation step without ever inspecting the actual schema. The prompt requires a verification step before plan finalization.
Variation: when the prototype has multiple consumers already, the plan should include backwards-compat shims at the SDK boundary.
Companion: [[overnight-hardening-pass]] is what you run AFTER this plan is approved and you want to land each phase incrementally.

name: jonny-ive-ux-review
purpose: Run a 'put on your Jony Ive design hat' thorough UX review that identifies opportunities to enrich/remove/simplify, generates feature ideas tied to research/M&A workflow, and applies the H9 design system for cross-app visual consistency.
contextRequired: Running prototype or screenshot of current UX
H9 design system tokens (h9-brand.css)
Context on the workflow the tool supports (research, M&A, etc.)
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: UX review memo + applied H9 design changes
purposeBody: A persona-driven UX review where the model is explicitly asked to think with Jony Ive's enrich/remove/simplify discipline, surface specific opportunities, AND apply the H9 design system. The combination of persona + workflow context + brand system makes the output specific rather than generic.
whenToUse: **Use when:** a prototype is working but needs design polish before it goes to partners.
**Use when:** you want the same review pass to also produce the cross-app brand alignment.
**Don't use when:** the brand system isn't established — apply [[h9-default-applied-everywhere]] first.
verbatim: decent start. put on your jonny ive design hat and do an thorough UX review, identify opportunity to enrich/remove/simplify, and think through key features and UX improvements that could make the tool more useful to my partners and I during {{WORKFLOW}}. Also, apply the H9 Design system so the app has the same look and feel as our other proejcts/apps
parameterized:
You are a senior product designer wearing the Jony Ive enrich/remove/simplify hat. You will produce both a written review AND apply code changes — but in separate commits so each can be evaluated independently.

Guardrails (do NOT exceed):
- Do not modify backend / data layer
- Do not introduce new dependencies
- Do not change information architecture (route structure) without flagging it as a separate decision

Review {{TOOL_NAME}}. Memo format (markdown file at {{MEMO_PATH}}):

## Enrich
Markdown table: `| Target screen/component | Change | Effort (S/M/L) | Screen reference |`

## Remove
Same table shape — what to cut, why it doesn't earn its pixels.

## Simplify
Same table shape — what to streamline (density, depth, decision count).

## Open IA decisions
List anything that would require route/IA changes — surface, don't apply.

Then apply the H9 design system via {{CSS_TOKEN_PATH}}:
- Fonts: Big Shoulders Display 800 weight on headlines, Inter on body, JetBrains Mono on tabular data
- Orange (#FF8C00) 3px rule with glow `box-shadow: 0 0 12px rgba(255,140,0,0.35)` under ≥1 section heading
- Pulsing orange dot on ≥1 eyebrow label
- Navy (#142338) logo mark with 1.5px orange border in top-left at ~36px
- Match overall feel of {{REFERENCE_APP}}

Commit memo first, then code changes second (separate commits).
adaptingNote: When adapting: for non-H9 brands, swap the tokens path and signature elements; keep the enrich/remove/simplify + separate-commits discipline.
exampleOutput: A review memo identifying 4 enrich, 3 remove, 5 simplify opportunities for a research tool; followed by code changes that swap in the H9 type stack, apply the navy/orange palette via CSS variables, drop in the orange rule + pulsing dot eyebrow pattern, and add a logo mark in the top-left. Two commits: `style: apply H9 design system` and `feat: enrich/simplify UX per design review`.

Coverage.text: Three sections (enrich / remove / simplify) each populated
H9 design system applied (fonts, palette, signature elements)
Each suggestion tagged with effort estimate (S/M/L)

Sourcing.text: Suggestions reference specific screens/components by name
Generic UX platitudes ("improve accessibility") without a concrete target
Replacing brand colors with off-spec hex values

Format.text: Review memo and code changes in separate commits (verify: `git log` shows ≥2 commits with distinct subjects)
Memo at `{{MEMO_PATH}}` contains all four required sections (Enrich, Remove, Simplify, Open IA decisions)
Orange 3px rule with glow under ≥1 section heading (grader greps CSS for `box-shadow.*255.*140.*0`)
Pulsing orange dot animation on ≥1 eyebrow label
Navy logo mark with 1.5px orange border present in top-left at ~36px
No new dependencies added (grader diffs package.json)
No backend file modifications (grader diffs api/, server/, db/ paths)
Before/after screenshots in the PR description if changes are visual

variations: "Jony Ive design hat" is the load-bearing persona. Variations tried: Dieter Rams (works for industrial-design-leaning UIs), Susan Kare (works for iconography reviews). Stick to one persona per review.
Companion: [[h9-default-applied-everywhere]] is the global setting that prevents you from having to re-specify the design system in every prompt.
**Anti-pattern observed:** model sometimes generates a generic UX critique with H9 colors slapped on. Eval should reject if specific screen names aren't present.

name: h9-default-applied-everywhere
purpose: One-time directive that commits a global brand-default behavior to memory: every PPT/HTML/XLS/PDF artifact applies H9 design guidelines by default unless overridden — eliminating the need to re-prompt branding per output.
contextRequired: H9 brand assets (CSS tokens, PDF guidelines, PPTX templates)
Persistent memory enabled in the session
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Memory entry + acknowledgment confirmation
purposeBody: Many sessions produce multi-format deliverables (PPT + Excel + PDF + markdown), and re-specifying the brand system every time is wasted tokens and a source of drift. This prompt sets a single persistent rule: H9 brand is the default, every output, every time, unless the user explicitly overrides. This is the one prompt in the library that's a setting-changer, not a task-runner.
whenToUse: **Use when:** starting a new project that will generate many cross-format artifacts.
**Use when:** a global CLAUDE.md isn't yet present and you want session-scoped enforcement.
**Don't use when:** the project should NOT default to H9 (e.g. third-party client work, neutral templates).
verbatim: every material in PPT, HTML, XLS, PDF, And other popular file formats should apply the h9 design guidelines and system by default and unless I override. Change your settings and commit that request to memory so it applies to this and future claude sessions
parameterized:
You are configuring a persistent memory/settings rule for a brand-default behavior. Act as a memory steward: keep the rule thin (reference paths to the brand assets, do not inline tokens that may drift).

Every material in {{FORMAT_LIST}} should apply the {{BRAND_SYSTEM}} design guidelines by default unless I override. Change your settings and commit that request to memory so it applies to this and future {{ASSISTANT}} sessions.

The {{BRAND_SYSTEM}} brand assets live at:
- Tokens (source of truth for code/web): {{CSS_PATH}}
- Guidelines PDF: {{PDF_PATH}}
- Templates (PPTX): {{PPTX_PATH}}

Overrides I may use:
- "plain markdown" or "no styling" — drop brand styling
- "use {{OTHER_BRAND}} branding instead" — switch brand systems (e.g., Vesper Aviation)
- "match {{REFERENCE_DOC}}" — copy styling from a specific reference document
- "brand-neutral" — strip all brand markings (for third-party deliverables)

Memory entry should:
- Reference the asset paths, NOT inline the tokens
- List every override pattern so override behavior is unambiguous
- Be confirmed back to me with the exact rule text and the path the rule was saved to

After saving, confirm with: "Saved to <path>. Default applies to {{FORMAT_LIST}}. Overrides: <list>."
adaptingNote: When adapting: for client-facing assistants, swap the override patterns for the client's branding terminology. The reference-paths-not-inline-tokens discipline is the same.
exampleOutput: The model writes a memory entry (e.g. in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or via a memory tool) capturing the H9 default with the brand-asset paths and the override patterns. Then confirms back: "Saved. Every PPT/HTML/XLS/PDF/DOCX/Markdown deliverable will apply H9 styling by default. Overrides supported: plain markdown, Vesper Aviation branding, match-an-existing-doc, brand-neutral."

Coverage.text: Memory entry created — verify with `grep -c "{{BRAND_SYSTEM}}" {{MEMORY_FILE}}` returning ≥1, OR the assistant's memory tool query for "brand default" returning the entry
All listed formats covered (PPT, HTML, XLS, PDF, DOCX, Markdown) — explicit count in the saved entry
Override patterns explicitly enumerated in the entry — grader counts ≥4 patterns
Confirmation response includes the exact saved file path and the rule text
Brand-asset paths referenced (not inlined) — grader greps for hex tokens (#FF8C00, #142338) in the memory entry; presence = fail

Sourcing.text: Brand asset paths verified to exist before writing the memory entry
Writing brand specifics into the memory entry (those live in the assets — keep memory thin)

Format.text: Confirmation message lists what was saved
Confirmation includes the override patterns so the user knows the escape hatches

variations: This is intentionally a directive, not a workflow. Expect ~1 prompt per project setup, then never again.
For project-level (not user-level) enforcement, put the same rules in the project's `CLAUDE.md`.
The Vesper Aviation portfolio exception: H9 is the default, but the user can say "this is for Vesper" and the brand switches. Make sure the memory entry knows that escape hatch.
**Anti-pattern observed:** model writes the H9 colors directly into the memory entry, which leads to drift when h9-brand.css updates. The eval enforces "reference paths, don't inline tokens."

name: layout-feedback-numbered-fixes
purpose: Send a single, numbered, multi-issue UI feedback message that combines visual polish (contrast, color), interaction polish (popups, explanations), and historical-state restoration ('bring back scenario X') — and asks for an audit of the restored state.
contextRequired: Running app or screenshot
Prior scenario/state context for the restoration request
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Multi-fix patch + audit summary of the restored state
purposeBody: The "I have 3 unrelated things to fix and I want them all done now" pattern. Numbered list of fixes spanning visual issues, interaction issues, and historical-state restoration, all in one message. The audit-the-restored-state step is the key: it forces the model to confirm the restored scenario actually matches the original intent.
whenToUse: **Use when:** you have ≥3 small fixes that don't justify separate prompts.
**Use when:** one of the fixes involves restoring a prior version that may have data integrity concerns.
**Don't use when:** a single fix is complex enough to need its own conversation — split it out.
parameterized:
You are a frontend engineer handling a multi-fix request. One of the fixes may involve restoring historical state from source control — restore from git history or saved files, NEVER from your own memory of the prior state.

Fix the following, in one commit per fix:

1. {{FIX_1_DESCRIPTION}} ({{FIX_1_TYPE}}: visual / contrast / typography)
2. {{FIX_2_DESCRIPTION}} ({{FIX_2_TYPE}}: interaction / tooltip / state)
3. {{FIX_3_DESCRIPTION}} ({{FIX_3_TYPE}}: restoration / new feature / refactor)

If Fix 3 is a restoration:
- Name the restored state "{{RESTORED_STATE_NAME}}"
- Include all prior artifacts/outputs from that state (pull from git history, not memory)
- After restoring, audit the restored state — confirm data, visualizations, and details are accurate

End with an audit memo enumerating: (a) every field you verified, (b) the source commit/file for each verified field, (c) any discrepancies found.

Where {{COMPARISON_PAIR}} = the two states/scenarios you want side-by-side after restoration (e.g., "pre-rotation vs post-rotation", "baseline vs optimized", "Active Planes First vs Santa Ana"). If no restoration is requested, drop the COMPARISON_PAIR clause and treat Fix 3 like any other fix.
adaptingNote: When adapting: for backend bug-bundle requests, swap the visual-fix examples for query-fix examples but keep the audit-the-restored-state discipline if any fix is a revert.
exampleOutput: A patch that: (1) updates link color in the first column from `#3366cc` to a higher-contrast token-defined color, (2) adds a tooltip on the Status column explaining the state machine on click, (3) restores the pre-rotation "Active Planes First" scenario as a selectable entry alongside "Santa Ana", with prior artifacts re-attached. Ends with an audit memo confirming the Active Planes First data is consistent: 73 airplanes placed, matching the original output.

Coverage.text: Every numbered fix addressed (no silent skip)
Restored scenario named exactly as specified
Audit summary at the end with explicit data-integrity confirmations

Sourcing.text: Restored artifacts traced to the original commit/version
Recreating restored data from memory — it must come from source (git history, saved file, backup)

Format.text: Audit memo enumerates which fields it verified
Each numbered fix maps to a separate commit or clearly-labeled change

variations: The "Audit the X to make sure the data, visualizations/schematics, and details are right" closer is the discipline that prevents silent regressions.
Variation: when the restoration step is complex, split it into its own prompt and use this pattern for the smaller fixes only.

**Anti-pattern observed:** model occasionally "restores" data from its own memory of the original scenario rather than from source. The eval should fail if the patch doesn't reference the source commit/file.

name: recreate-deck-with-changes
purpose: Rebuild a slide deck after underlying data/parameters have changed, verifying that toggleable features (e.g. served parking on/off) are now applied to every scenario, with dimensions and research outputs visible.
contextRequired: Existing deck template / generation pipeline
Updated parameter settings
H9 design system for PPTX
sourceSession: Vesper KSNA site plan deck, May 2026
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Regenerated PPTX with all changes applied
purposeBody: After a scenario-model change, the slide deck is out of sync. This prompt regenerates the deck, explicitly toggles a known parameter ON for all scenarios (so a prior bug where it was on only for one is fixed), and surfaces both dimensions and supporting research in the visible artifact.
whenToUse: **Use when:** the deck is downstream of a parametric model and the model has changed.
**Use when:** there's a known prior bug (e.g. a flag was on for some but not all scenarios) that the regeneration should explicitly fix.
**Don't use when:** the deck doesn't have a generation pipeline — manual edits won't reproduce this prompt's value.
verbatim: recreate the {{DECK_NAME}} so I can see how everything looks after all the changes. be sure to turn {{TOGGLE_FEATURE}} on for all {{N}} scenarios. i also want to be able to see the {{ADDITIONAL_DETAIL_1}} and the results of your research when it comes to {{ADDITIONAL_DETAIL_2}}.

You are a deck regeneration assistant working from a parametric model. Before regenerating, list the scenarios you found and the toggle states you intend to set, then proceed.

Recreate {{DECK_NAME}} with the changes from {{CHANGE_SOURCE}} applied.

Required toggles:
- Turn {{TOGGLE_FEATURE}} ON for all {{N}} scenarios (no exceptions)

Required content per scenario slide:
- {{ADDITIONAL_DETAIL_1}} (visible on the slide, not just in notes)
- {{ADDITIONAL_DETAIL_2}} with sourced research outputs

Design system: {{DESIGN_SYSTEM}} (default H9; use Vesper if {{AUDIENCE}} is a Vesper deliverable).

Deliverable: {{OUTPUT_PATH}} as PPTX.

exampleOutput: A regenerated `KSNA Site Plan Deck.pptx` with: served parking turned ON for all 3 scenarios (previously only on for Santa Ana), each scenario's dimensions visible on its slide, and a new appendix slide with parking-space-design research outputs (FAA AC 150/5300-13B references, real-world space-per-aircraft data).

Coverage.text: Toggle parameter is ON for every scenario (not just one)
Dimensions visible on each scenario slide
Supporting research appears in the deck (not just referenced)
H9 design system applied (navy/orange/Big Shoulders Display)

Sourcing.text: Each research claim has a citation (FAA AC, ICAO, etc.)
Made-up dimension values not from the parametric model

Format.text: PPTX format saved at the specified `{{OUTPUT_PATH}}`
Title font on every slide is Big Shoulders Display, weight 800
Orange (#FF8C00) 3pt rule under every slide title — grader greps the XML for `<a:ln w="38100"><a:solidFill><a:srgbClr val="FF8C00"/>`
H9 logo mark (navy square, orange border) appears on every content slide
Cover slide background is navy (#142338) with the orange 40px grid overlay
Confidentiality footer present if `{{AUDIENCE}}` is external

Pre-flight verification.text: Before regenerating, model output lists every scenario found and the toggle state intended for each — grader verifies count matches `{{N}}`

variations: **Anti-pattern observed:** the model applies the toggle to only the scenarios that match its prior mental model and silently skips the rest. The "turn X on for ALL scenarios" framing + the pre-flight verification eval line prevents this.
**Failure mode:** stale slides from prior renders remain in the deck (e.g., pre-rotation Zone slides) — watch for ordering mismatches between the model and the deck.
**Anti-pattern observed:** the model generates an entirely new deck when it should regenerate the existing one. The prompt should reference the source deck path explicitly when this risk exists.

Companion: [[pdf-to-html-revenue-section]] handles the inverse — when a deliverable is missing data that exists in a source doc.

name: pdf-to-html-revenue-section
purpose: Diagnose why a generated HTML deliverable is missing a section that exists in a source PDF (e.g. revenue breakdown by product) — and either explain the omission or fix it.
contextRequired: Source PDF path with the data
Generated HTML deliverable
The pipeline / generator code that produced the HTML
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Diagnostic explanation + patch (if fixable) OR a clear 'why this can't be done' note
purposeBody: When a generator script consumed a source PDF but a downstream HTML is missing a section the PDF contains, the prompt asks for the *why* first (not a silent fix). This forces the model to inspect the pipeline rather than re-generate, which is how silent data drops happen.
whenToUse: **Use when:** a generated artifact is missing data the source clearly contains.
**Use when:** you want to know if it's a parser bug, an extraction bug, or a deliberate filter.
**Don't use when:** the section was never expected to be in the output — that's a feature request, not a diagnostic.
verbatim: {{SUPPLIER}} supplied a document ("{{PDF_NAME}}") with {{DATA_TYPE}} for {{YEAR}}. the html doesn't include the {{MISSING_SECTION}} in the "{{HTML_SECTION_NAME}}" section. Why?
parameterized:
You are a pipeline-debugging engineer. Diagnose first, do not regenerate. Do not edit any files yet — propose patches only.

Context:
- Source document: {{SOURCE_PATH}} ({{SOURCE_TYPE}}, e.g., PDF/XLSX/CSV)
- Expected data in source: {{EXPECTED_DATA_TYPE}} for {{SCOPE}} (e.g., "revenue by product for 2025")
- Generated artifact: {{GENERATED_PATH}} ({{GENERATED_TYPE}}, e.g., HTML report)
- Missing in artifact: the {{MISSING_SECTION}} that should appear in the {{ARTIFACT_SECTION_NAME}} section

Walk through the pipeline in this order — do not skip steps:
1. Extraction: open the source, confirm the data is actually present, note page/section
2. Transform: inspect any aggregation, filtering, or schema mapping between source and artifact
3. Render: inspect the template/component that should display the section
4. Conclude: state the root cause with file:line citation

Then return:
- (1) Root cause with file:line
- (2) Source page/section where the data lives (verified)
- (3) ≥2 fix options with effort estimate (S/M/L)
- (4) Recommendation among options with stated reason

End with: "I have not edited any files. Approve an option and I'll patch."
adaptingNote: When adapting: for non-PDF sources, swap the OCR/extraction step; for non-HTML artifacts, inspect the equivalent renderer.
exampleOutput: "Looked at the pipeline. name: ingest-email-feedback-plan
purpose: Ingest an email/comms document containing client feedback items, understand each item, and produce a plan that addresses each — explicitly flagging items the model cannot auto-handle and explaining what the human needs to do.
contextRequired: Path to the email/comms file (.eml, .pdf, or markdown)
Context on the project being given feedback
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Plan with per-item action + a 'manual needed' list
purposeBody: Take a piece of feedback that's structured by the giver (numbered or bulleted) and produce a parallel action plan — one row per feedback item — with an explicit can-handle vs cannot-handle column. The cannot-handle items are the actual handoff.
whenToUse: **Use when:** feedback came in as a single document and you want to translate it into a work list.
**Use when:** some items are likely outside the model's reach (need credentials, need new design assets, need stakeholder buy-in).
**Don't use when:** feedback is ambiguous and needs a clarification round first.
verbatim: @{{FEEDBACK_FILE_PATH}} ingest, understand, and create a plan for addressing each of the feedback items {{AUTHOR}} documented in the email. note any change that you cannot automatically handle and explain what I need to do instead.
parameterized:
You are an execution-planning assistant. Your job is to translate feedback into a parallel action list with explicit handoffs. Plan only — do not execute any of the can-handle items in this turn.

@{{FEEDBACK_FILE_PATH}}

Ingest and produce the plan as a single markdown table with these exact columns:

| # | Original item (quoted) | Status | Planned action | Effort | Confidence | Manual needed? |
|---|------------------------|--------|----------------|--------|------------|----------------|

Where:
- Status ∈ {Can handle, Cannot handle, Ambiguous}
- Effort ∈ {S, M, L}
- Confidence ∈ {High, Medium, Low — and reason if Low}
- Manual needed? = Yes/No, and Yes rows feed the manual-needed section below

Followed by:

## Manual needed
A separate list collapsing every Cannot handle and Ambiguous row. For each: a "what I need from you" sentence the user can act on.

## Plan-only commitment
End with: "I have not executed any item. Approve the Can-handle rows and I'll proceed."
adaptingNote: When adapting: for verbal feedback (transcripts), first run a "structure into discrete items" pass, then apply this prompt to the structured output.
exampleOutput: A plan listing each of the author's items as a row: `1. Change hero copy → Can handle, S effort, will draft 2 variants for review. 2. New logo from designer → Cannot handle, M effort, need final logo file from designer. 3. Site password protection → Can handle, S effort, via Netlify. 4. Add testimonials → Ambiguous (which testimonials?), Cannot handle until clarified.` Ends with a "manual needed" list collapsing items 2 and 4.

Coverage.text: Every numbered item in the source feedback has a row in the plan
Can-handle vs Cannot-handle decision on each item
"Manual needed" section enumerating cannot-handle items at the end
Ambiguous items flagged separately from cannot-handle items

Sourcing.text: Each plan row quotes or paraphrases the original feedback line
Plan items not in the source feedback (no scope creep)
Pretending to handle an item that requires external assets

Format.text: Output is a markdown table with the columns: `# | Original item | Status | Planned action | Effort | Confidence | Manual needed?`
"Manual needed" section after the table enumerating cannot-handle and ambiguous rows
Final line: "I have not executed any item. Approve the Can-handle rows and I'll proceed." — verbatim
Executing any can-handle item in this turn (eval fails if any file other than the plan output is modified)

variations: **Anti-pattern observed:** the model starts executing the easy can-handle items mid-plan, skipping user approval. The "Do not execute any of the can-handle items in this turn" guardrail + the verbatim closing line prevents this.

**Anti-pattern observed:** the model hand-waves cannot-handle items ("we'll figure that out") without a concrete "what I need from you" sentence. The "explain what I need to do instead" closer is load-bearing — watch for it.
**Failure mode:** ambiguous items get auto-classified as Can handle, then fail silently in execution. The Ambiguous column value + Confidence column catches this.

**Don't use when:** the registry already exposes a clean filter (e.g. SEC's CIK lookup) — just use the API.

Famous in a general sense rather than celebrity one as I'm looking for well known business people, movie celebrities, politicians, or anybody consequential within the US."

You are a data-engineering planner curating a derived dataset from a public registry. Before drafting the schema, write the filter's qualifying examples and disqualifying examples — let those drive the schema fields. The operational filter is the load-bearing decision; the schema follows.

Inventing plausible-sounding skill names that don't exist in the catalog

name: data-trust-assurance
purpose: Update a skill to never round dimensions, fetch a critical missing field for every record, and explicitly mandate trusted-source-only data — replacing prior seed/synthetic data with verified data and getting assurance language in the skill itself.
contextRequired: Existing skill that handles aircraft (or similar) dimensions
Trusted-source roster (manufacturer specs, FAA TC data sheets)
author: Daniel
outputArtifact: Updated skill with no-rounding rule + tail-height field + trust assurance
purposeBody: A meta-prompt for hardening a skill's data integrity: forbid rounding, require a new field (tail height), and explicitly worry about "seed" data that the skill may have generated as placeholder — the prompt forces the model to either retire the seed values or vouch for them with sources.
whenToUse: **Use when:** a skill produces dimension-sensitive output and rounding errors compound downstream.
**Use when:** you suspect a skill carries synthetic/seed data forward into production.
**Don't use when:** the skill is read-only against a verified source — there's nothing to harden.
verbatim: update the skill to never round up or down on any of the dimensions. Also, we need {{NEW_REQUIRED_FIELD}} for all {{ENTITY_TYPES}} we retrieve. also, i'm nervous about whatever data was created by seed or referred to as seed. implies the {{ENTITY_TYPE_DIMENSION}} data is untrustworthy. I need assurance that the dimension data we use go forward is trusted, accurate, and never manipulated
parameterized:
You are a data-integrity engineer hardening a skill. Before editing the skill code, enumerate every place rounding could occur (extraction, transform, presentation) and address each. Do not silently replace seed values with regenerated synthetic data and call it verified — every replacement must cite a verifiable source URL or document.

Update {{SKILL_NAME}} with the following data-integrity requirements:

1. NEVER round any dimension value — preserve full precision from source through to storage; rounding only at presentation, never in stored data
2. Always populate {{NEW_REQUIRED_FIELD}} for every {{ENTITY_TYPE}} record
3. Replace ALL seed/synthetic/placeholder values with verified data from {{TRUSTED_SOURCES}}
4. Add a `source` field to every record citing the manufacturer spec / TC data sheet / authoritative document

Update the skill description to explicitly mandate trusted-source-only data and require a source citation per record.

Confirm back with this exact table format:

| record_id | prior_status (seed / synthetic / verified) | new_status (verified / unverified) | source_url_or_doc | notes |
|-----------|--------------------------------------------|------------------------------------|-------------------|-------|

End with a summary line: "Replaced X seed records; Y now verified; Z remain unverified and flagged."

exampleOutput: The skill is updated with: precision preservation throughout the pipeline, tail-height column added (sourced from FAA Type Certificate Data Sheets), all prior seed dimensions replaced with manufacturer data, a `source` column per record citing the URL/document. Confirmation lists: "32 records had seed data, all replaced; 28 verified against manufacturer; 4 verified against FAA TCDS; 0 records remain unverified." Skill description now includes the no-seed mandate.

New required field populated for every record
All prior seed data either replaced or explicitly flagged
Source citation per record

Sourcing.text: Trusted sources named (manufacturer, FAA TCDS, etc.)
Re-introducing rounding "for display purposes" without preserving precise values in storage
Synthetic / regenerated data presented as verified

Format.text: Skill description updated to reflect the new mandate
Audit returned as a markdown table with columns: `record_id | prior_status | new_status | source_url_or_doc | notes`
Summary line at the end with counts (X seed → Y verified → Z unverified)
Skill description includes a confidence threshold for accepted sources

contextRequired: Path to the new CSV export
Path to the previous export for diff (optional)
Cutoff months for staleness check
author: Jake
outputArtifact: Data-quality report enumerating findings by row number
purposeBody: A fresh batch of sale or lease comps just landed and you want a sanity sweep for impossible values, airport-code mismatches, unit drift, and stale rows before the estimator consumes it. Airport-code accuracy is sacred at H9 (per DESIGN.md §Aviation conventions) — one T67-mislabeled-as-KCHD row that leaks into the comp pool will give a customer a confidently-wrong H9 Hangars Estimate.
whenToUse: **Use when:** a new CSV export has landed and is about to be ingested into the formula.
**Use when:** an estimator output looks wrong and you suspect upstream data drift.
**Don't use when:** the data is from a verified manufacturer / TC source — there's nothing to spot-check.
verbatim: Spot-check the comp dataset at {{CSV_PATH}} before it lands in the estimator.
parameterized:
Spot-check the comp dataset at {{CSV_PATH}} before it lands in the estimator.

Compare against the previous export at {{PREVIOUS_CSV}} (if provided).

Produce a report with exactly these sections:

1. **Row counts**
   - Total rows now vs. previous
   - Closed (usable) vs. open/listing rows
   - Count per airport (top 10)

2. **Airport-code integrity**
   - Any row where the city/state column does not match the airport-code home. Quote the row.
   - Any row mixing codes from different metros (KCHD + T67 in one record, etc.)

3. **Unit & value sanity**

   - Any rows with sqft <100 or >50,000

Airport-code integrity section enumerates every mismatch with row number
Empty sections marked `Clean.` not omitted

Findings without a row reference
Inventing issues to fill an otherwise-clean section

name: claude-scope-recovery
purpose: Pull Claude back to scope when mid-task it has started "helpfully" refactoring, adding error handling for impossible states, or expanding the change beyond what you asked for. One-shot correction that re-anchors without burning the session.
contextRequired: The current diff or working state where scope expansion happened
The original task as stated
author: Jake
outputArtifact: Reverted diff + a one-phrase drift category + continued original work
purposeBody: Mid-task, Claude has started "helpfully" refactoring, adding error handling for impossible states, or expanding the change beyond what you asked for. You want a one-shot correction that re-anchors without burning the session. A blunt, structured correction works better than a vague "stay focused" nudge — naming the drift pattern by category (defensive code, abstraction, future-proofing) teaches the model the shape of what to avoid for the rest of the session.
whenToUse: **Use when:** Claude added code you didn't ask for in the same response as code you did.
**Use when:** you want to teach the session the drift pattern so it self-corrects later.
**Don't use when:** the expansion is genuinely needed — accept it and revise the task.
verbatim: Stop. You've expanded scope beyond what I asked for. Here's what's extra: {{paste extras}}. Original ask: {{original task}}. Revert and continue.
parameterized:
Stop. You've expanded scope beyond what I asked for.

Specifically, you added:
{{paste 1–3 examples of the drift — defensive code for impossible states, a new abstraction, error handling I didn't ask for, a backwards-compat shim, etc.}}

The original task was: {{restate the original ask in one sentence.}}

Do this, in order:
1. Revert the unrequested additions. Show me the diff you're keeping vs. dropping.
2. Name the drift category in one phrase (defensive code / premature abstraction / future-proofing / unrequested refactor / scope creep).
3. Continue ONLY with the original task.

No apology. No "thanks for catching that." No restating the rule back to me. Just the diff and one phrase.
adaptingNote: When adapting: for runaway research (model went off on tangent context-gathering), substitute "revert the side-quest reading" for the diff step.
exampleOutput: "Reverted: removed `try/catch` block around the call (impossible state), removed the new `EstimateCache` class (abstraction not asked for). Drift category: defensive code. Continuing the original task: add the per-tier confidence pill to the result card."

Coverage.text: Diff is reverted to original ask scope
Drift category named in one phrase
Original task is continued (not abandoned)

Sourcing.text: The reverted additions are listed explicitly so the user can verify
Apology theater ("thanks for catching that", "you're right") in the response

Format.text: Short response — diff + one phrase + continuation. No essay.

variations: Promote to `production` after 3 sessions where this prompt successfully prevented further drift.
Companion: [[skill-discovery-question]] when the drift was "I'll just write a custom thing" but a skill already exists.

Repo's recent CHANGELOG entries (for voice matching)

You want a PR description that tells the reviewer (Dad, or your future self) what changed, why, and how to verify — plus a one-line changelog entry that matches the repo's voice. PRs without an explicit Test Plan get reviewed shallowly. A checklist forces both author and reviewer to walk the change.

**Use when:** the diff is small enough to summarize in 3 bullets — if not, the PR should probably be split.
**Don't use when:** the branch hasn't been tested — fix that first.

(3 bullets max. Each starts with a verb. No "various improvements.")

- [ ] (another)

CHANGELOG line voice matches the last 5 entries (verb-led, present tense)
Marketing language ("enhanced experience", "various improvements")

author: Jake

purposeBody: You or Dad have a half-formed feature idea ("we should let airport managers see who's on the waitlist") and want it shaped into a spec that matches the style of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` / `ESTIMATOR_SPEC.md` before any engineering planning. Explicit non-goals + an Open Questions section prevent scope creep and force surface-level ambiguities to the top instead of burying them in implementation.

**Use when:** before any engineering planning — the spec frames the design, the design constrains the math.
**Don't use when:** the spec already exists — extend it rather than restart.

I have a rough feature idea for {{PROJECT}}. Turn it into a structured spec matching the style of {{REFERENCE_SPEC_PATH}} in this repo.

Idea: {{ROUGH_IDEA}}

Produce these sections, in order:
1. Problem (1 paragraph — whose pain, how acute, evidence)
2. Goals (3–5 bullets, each measurable)
3. Non-goals (3+ bullets — what we are explicitly NOT solving)
4. Primary user & job-to-be-done (1 sentence in JTBD form)

≥3 open questions enumerated

Engineering implementation details (DB schemas, API shapes) in this spec

Format.text: Markdown with the 7 required H2/H3 sections
Length 600–1200 words

name: boss-status-update-from-session
purpose: Convert a working session's git activity / completed-and-slipped todos / unilateral decisions into a four-section status update for an absent manager — shipped, decided-without-you, needs-your-eyes, new-ideas — short enough to read on a phone.
contextRequired: Today's git log on the relevant branch (or PR list)
Tasks/todos completed and slipped during the session
Any decisions made unilaterally that the manager would want to know about
author: Jake
outputArtifact: Markdown message, ~150–250 words, four H3 sections
purposeBody: When the manager is unavailable for a day (sick child, surgery, travel) and you're working solo, the right artifact is not a meeting recap — it's a phone-readable status update they can scan in 90 seconds when they get a free moment. This prompt produces exactly that: four sections, plain prose, no headers-for-headers'-sake, and a bias toward decisions and asks over narrative.
whenToUse: **Use when:** the manager has been out of pocket for a day or longer and you owe him a wrap-up he can read on his phone.
**Use when:** you made one or more judgment calls on his behalf and want them documented for an asymmetric "speak now or hold your peace" review.
**Don't use when:** the day was routine and a one-line Slack message would suffice — this prompt is for days with real decisions.
**Don't use when:** you need a deep narrative retrospective — use a different prompt for that.
verbatim:
Write me a status update for my manager. He was out today for a family medical thing. Keep it short — phone-readable, ~200 words.

Four sections, in this order:
1. **Shipped today.** Concrete artifacts only — file paths, commit SHAs, PR links. No verbs like "worked on".
2. **Decided without you.** Anything I picked unilaterally that you'd reasonably want a vote on. One line each, with the rationale in a half-sentence.
3. **Needs your eyes.** Things I can't unblock myself: design calls, account/credential issues, anything cross-org.
4. **New ideas (low priority).** 1–3 bullets max, things worth a 30-second look later but not urgent.

Rules:
- No emojis. No "Hope grandma's surgery went well" — he'll know I care without me saying it.
- No padding. If a section has nothing real, write "Nothing today" and move on.
- Lead with the most reversible item in "Decided without you" so he doesn't have to read the whole list to find what matters.
adaptingNote: When adapting: when the manager is on vacation (multi-day, not one-day), swap section 4 ("New ideas") for "Held for your return" — things you intentionally paused so they don't get litigated async.
exampleOutput: Four H3 sections totaling ~200 words. 'Shipped today' has 2–4 bullets, each anchored by a commit SHA, file path, or PR URL. 'Decided without you' has 1–3 one-liners, each with a half-sentence rationale, lead bullet being the most easily reversed. 'Needs your eyes' has 1–3 items with the exact ask ("share PROMPT_IQ_KEY", "confirm SIVEF transferability"). 'New ideas' has 1–3 short bullets — not urgent, not justified, just captured.

Coverage.text: All four sections present, in the specified order
'Shipped today' contains at least one concrete artifact reference (file path, SHA, PR URL, named doc) OR the literal phrase 'Nothing today'
'Decided without you' lists unilateral decisions with a rationale half-sentence each

Sourcing.text: Every 'Shipped' item is verifiable from the raw material provided (no invented work)
Padding sympathies ('hope X is okay') — the manager already knows you care
Verbs like 'worked on', 'investigated', 'started' in the Shipped section — only completed artifacts

Format.text: Markdown with four H3 sections, headings exactly as specified
Total length within ±20% of the word budget
'Decided without you' leads with the most reversible item

variations: Anti-pattern: the model wants to write a narrative paragraph at the top before the sections. Cut it — managers reading on phones scroll past it.
Anti-pattern: the model conflates 'shipped' with 'started'. Strict eval on 'completed artifact only' prevents this.
Companion: [[ingest-email-feedback-plan]] when the day's work was reactive to a long manager message rather than self-directed.
Companion: [[pr-description-and-changelog]] if 'Shipped today' is dominated by a single PR — the PR description doubles as the artifact link.
